Saiga antelope (Saiga tatarica) exhibit a pronounced sexual dimorphism in neonatal mass, a pattern consistent with the species' highly polygynous mating system. Female calves typically emerge at a wet weight of 3450 grams [Wwb = 3450 grams], whereas their male counterparts are born at a substantially heavier 3700 grams [Wwb = 3700 grams]. This disparity at parturition likely reflects differential maternal investment, as male calves possess a greater capacity for early competitive growth. Recorded under a core body temperature typical of healthy, active saiga (39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C]), the gestation period for female calves averages 152 days [tg = 152 days]. This duration represents a compressed pregnancy relative to many other bovids of comparable adult size, an adaptation thought to be linked to the species' migratory habits and the need to synchronize birth with the brief pulse of spring vegetation on the Eurasian steppe. The timing of parturition is thus a critical life-history variable, tightly coupled with environmental seasonality and the mother's physiological condition. Under these same thermal conditions, females produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], with an average of 1.7 calves per litter [N_R_i = 1.7 calves per litter].

Following the initial neonatal period, the transition to nutritional independence unfolds over a carefully timed interval. At a standard body temperature of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], the time since birth at weaning for saiga calves is 87 days [tx = 87 days]. During this suckling phase, the milk-dependent young gain mass rapidly, with the wet weight at weaning documented at 14,500 grams [Wwx = 14,500 grams]. This weaning mass represents a substantial increase from birth weight, reflecting the high energetic content of saiga milk and the intense maternal care provided during the spring and early summer. The relatively short weaning period is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid juvenile growth and dispersal, allowing females to rebuild their own body condition before the next breeding season. The timing of this nutritional transition is critical, as it must coincide with peak forage availability to ensure the post-weaning survival of the juvenile.

The species' reproductive output is constrained by its environment, with a maximum reproductive rate that is modest compared to other social ungulates. Under optimal thermal conditions (39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C]), females produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], with an average of 1.7 calves per litter [N_R_i = 1.7 calves per litter]. This annual litter size, slightly below two, represents a trade-off between offspring number and the high per-capita investment required to produce precocial calves capable of joining the migratory herd within days of birth. The twinning rate is variable, influenced by maternal age and body condition, with older, heavier females more likely to produce twins. This reproductive strategy, characterized by a single yearly event of moderate fecundity, is well-suited to a species that must contend with harsh, unpredictable steppe winters.

Onset of reproductive capability in saiga is markedly sex-specific, a pattern common in polygynous bovids where males delay maturation to invest more heavily in somatic growth. Under typical physiological conditions (39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C]), the time since birth at puberty for females is 331 days [tp = 331 days], meaning most females become capable of breeding before their first birthday. By contrast, males do not reach puberty until 669 days after birth [tp = 669 days after birth], roughly twice the period required by females at a temperature of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C]. This substantial delay reflects the intense intrasexual competition for mating opportunities, as older, larger males dominate breeding access during the rut. The consequence for population dynamics is a distinct generation time difference, with females contributing to recruitment much earlier than males. A female born early in the spring can, in principle, conceive during the autumn rut of the same calendar year, a strategy that maximizes lifetime reproductive output in a short-lived species.

The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult saiga underscores the marked sexual size dimorphism that defines the species. Males reach a maximum recorded body mass of 43,100 grams [Wwi = 43,100 grams], while adult females are considerably lighter, at 30,800 grams [Wwi = 30,800 grams]. This dimorphism, with males approximately 40% heavier than females, is among the most pronounced in the Bovidae and is a direct product of the polygynous mating system described earlier. At a core temperature of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], the maximum lifespan of this species is 16.3 years [am = 16.3 years], a relatively modest longevity for a bovid of this body size, likely constrained by the extreme environmental conditions of the steppe, regular disease outbreaks, and predation pressure. Field records indicate that few individuals in the wild approach this ceiling, with heavy mortality concentrated during harsh winters. The interplay between rapid sexual maturation, high adult mortality, and a compressed reproductive window thus shapes the saiga's overall life-history trajectory.
